extracted.intended_audience: patent classifiers / patent examiners / intellectual property office staff
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and criteria from the Guide to the International Patent Classification (IPC) for deciding how to classify patent documents, including when and where to assign classification symbols and indexing codes across different kinds of subject matter and publication stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus vs Process classification
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject of the invention concerns an apparatus, it is classified in the place for the apparatus if such a place exists. When such a place does not exist, the apparatus is classified in the place for the process performed by that apparatus. When the subject of the invention concerns a process for making or treatment of products, it is classified in the place for the process performed. When such a place does not exist, the making or treatment of products is classified in the place for the apparatus performing the process. If no place exists for the manufacture of a product, the manufacturing apparatus or process is classified in the place covering the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply apparatus-first when a dedicated place exists; otherwise use the process place and vice versa. The rule ensures inventions are placed where users will expect to find either the apparatus or the process that realizes the product. No special indexing note beyond these fallback rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articles of Manufacture classification
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject of the invention concerns an article, it is classified in the place for the article. If no place exists for the article itself, it is classified in the appropriate function-oriented place (i.e., according to the function performed by the article) or, if this is not possible, according to the field of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a glue-dispenser specially adapted for binding books is classified in B42C 9/00 (‘Applying glue or adhesive peculiar to bookbinding’) — because no specific place for glue-dispensers for bookbinding exists, classify by function ('applying glue'). Use function-oriented places before resorting to field-of-use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multistep processes and industrial plant classification
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject of the invention concerns a multistep process or an industrial plant consisting of a combination of process steps or apparatus, it is classified as a whole, i.e., in a place provided for such combination. If no such place exists, it is classified in the place for the product obtained by the process or plant. When the subject of the invention also concerns an element of the combination (for example an individual step or machine of the plant), the element is also separately classified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a group that covers the combination as a whole (e.g., subclass B09B). If absent, classify by product. Additionally classify novel inventive subelements separately (multiple classification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Details and constructional parts classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Details or parts only applicable to, or specially adapted for, one kind of subject matter are classified in the details places of this kind of subject matter, if such places exist; if such places do not exist, these details or parts are classified in the place for the subject matter in question. Details or parts applicable to more than one kind of subject matter are classified in the details places of more general nature, if such places exist; if such places of more general nature do not exist, these details or parts are classified according to all of the kinds of subject matter to which they explicitly apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow existence of dedicated 'details' groups first; otherwise classify with the main subject(s). Example: umbrella details applicable to more than one umbrella kind are in group 25/00; otherwise classify according to each applicable kind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of fully identified compounds from general chemical formulae (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification should be given to all 'fully identified' compounds that are novel and unobvious if they are: (i) specifically claimed as such or in a composition, (ii) products of a claimed process, or (iii) derivatives of either of these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A compound is 'fully identified' where the structure is given by exact chemical name or formula, or can be deduced from its preparation from specified reactants (not more than one selected from alternatives), and the compound is characterised by a physical property (e.g., melting point), or its preparation is described in a worked example with practical details. Compounds identified only by an empirical formula are not 'fully identified'. Classify each such fully identified novel/unobvious compound in the most specific groups that provide for them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification when no fully identified compounds are disclosed (Step 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If no 'fully identified' compounds are disclosed (e.g., compounds derived from computer-generated models and not experimentally verified), classification should only be given to compounds with exact chemical name or developed chemical formula. Classification should be limited to a single or a very small number of groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit classification breadth when compounds are speculative or not fully identified; avoid proliferating many classification symbols for hypothetical compounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification when only a general Markush formula is disclosed (Step 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: When only the general Markush formula is disclosed, classification is made in the most specific group(s) that cover(s) all or most of the potential embodiments. Classification should be limited to a single or a very small number of groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek the smallest set of groups that adequately cover most potential embodiments; avoid classifying into many highly specific places that would be impractical for searching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-obligatory classification for other compounds derived from general formulae (Step 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to obligatory classification of fully identified compounds, non-obligatory classification may be made when other compounds within the scope of the general formula, or compounds derived directly from computer-generated models, are of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classifier discretion may be used to add extra classifications for compounds of search interest; these are optional and intended to improve search coverage when warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting number of classification symbols for many fully identified compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: When classification of all the 'fully identified' compounds into their most specific classification places would lead to a high number of classification symbols (for example, more than twenty), the classifier may reduce the number of symbols. This may only be done when classification of the 'fully identified' compounds would lead to assigning a large number of subgroups under a single group at the next hierarchically higher level. Classification of these compounds may then be made in the higher group only. Otherwise, classification of the compounds is made in all of the more specific subgroups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this reduction only to avoid an excessive proliferation of near-duplicate subgroup symbols under one higher group; do not arbitrarily reduce specificity except in the stated situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of combinatorial libraries
rubrics_metrics.description: For collections ('libraries') composed of many chemical compounds, biological entities or other substances, only the individual members which are considered 'fully identified' are obligatorily classified into the groups that most specifically provide for them. The library as a whole is classified in an appropriate group in subclass C40B. In addition to obligatory classifications, non-obligatory classifications may be made when other members are of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid burdening the search system by classifying every library member; classify the library as a unit (C40B) and classify only fully identified members obligatorily. Optional indexing/classification may be applied for other members of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to apply multiple classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple classification of documents is necessary when the invention information relates to two or more inventive things that can each be classified in different groups (for example, alternative embodiments, or when a document relates to both a product and a process for its production and there are groups for both). Multiple classification should also be made when a single inventive thing is characterised by different aspects that are covered in different groups (construction, material, means for control, function-oriented vs application-oriented places).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply multiple classification to reflect distinct inventive things or distinct aspects useful for search. 105bis: multiple classification or classification combined with indexing is desirable to indicate additional searchable information. Check subclass-specific notes for more detailed multiple-classification guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of schemes for secondary classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary classification schemes are provided in certain areas to improve effectiveness; these schemes cover aspects partially or entirely covered elsewhere in the IPC and their symbols are always allocated in combination with classification symbols from other subclasses to enable complementary search by cross-combination of symbols. Symbols of schemes for secondary classification are not listed first when assigned as per paragraph 156(a). Notes in the schemes are authoritative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a secondary classification scheme exists for an aspect (examples provided in the Guide: A01P, A61P, A61Q, etc.), apply it in combination with the relevant primary classification symbols. Follow authoritative notes in those schemes carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid systems and indexing schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Hybrid systems consist of a classification scheme and an associated complementary indexing scheme. The indexing scheme specifies aspects not covered by classification places. When classifying within a hybrid system, first assign all appropriate classification symbols, then add appropriate indexing codes from associated indexing schemes if they identify elements useful for search purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indexing codes have formats similar to classification symbols and are placed after classification schemes (often starting at 101/00). Some subclasses are for indexing only and are indicated in titles. Indexing codes can only be applied in association with classification symbols; notes indicate where indexing codes may be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application and hierarchical use of indexing codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Indexing codes may be applied when it is desirable for search purposes to identify elements of information about a technical subject already classified as such. In an indexing scheme, the hierarchically higher group is only to be used in a residual manner to record specific features not provided for in subdivisions. When indexing two or more elements, for each element the hierarchically lowest indexing group which provides for this element should be applied. Indexing of residual matter in main groups should be limited, and indexing should not be made in main groups of very wide or general scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the most specific applicable indexing group; avoid using overly general indexing codes that give no useful search information. Example: in a welding process applicable to rails, beams and wheels, apply specific codes for rails and beams (101/26 and 101/28) rather than a too-general 101/00.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligatory classification of invention information
rubrics_metrics.description: According to Article 4(3) of the Strasbourg Agreement, when classifying a patent document, the competent authorities shall indicate 'the complete symbols of the Classification applied to the invention to which the patent document relates'. The interpretation is that it is an obligation to allot the classification symbols that represent invention information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always assign classification symbols representing invention information (i.e., the parts of the disclosure that are novel and unobvious and represent the invention) as obligatory classification. These take precedence over optional/additional classifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-obligatory classification and indexing of additional information
rubrics_metrics.description: It is desirable that additional information is classified or indexed when it is useful for search purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classifier discretion is used to add non-obligatory classification symbols or indexing codes to represent complementary or contextual information useful to searchers, but these are not required by the Strasbourg obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of patents granted after search and examination
rubrics_metrics.description: All subject matter covered by the claims of a patent document must be classified as invention information along with any novel and unobvious constituents or components (subcombinations) of the claimed subject matter. Classification should be based on the subject matter of each claim as a whole and on each inventive embodiment within a claim. Any unclaimed subject matter in the disclosure that is novel and unobvious must also be classified as invention information. It is desirable to classify or index any additional information complementing the invention information if useful for search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For granted patents, treat claims and novel/unobvious disclosed elements as invention information; include novel subcombinations. Also consider classifying complementary additional information where useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of searched but unexamined patent documents (e.g., published applications)
rubrics_metrics.description: All claimed subject matter that appears to be novel and unobvious in view of the search results must be classified as invention information along with any novel and unobvious constituents or components (subcombinations) of the claimed subject matter. Any unclaimed subject matter in the disclosure that appears to be novel and unobvious in view of the search results must also be classified as invention information. It is desirable to classify or index any additional information complementing the invention information if useful for search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the search results to determine novelty/unobviousness for classification decisions on published but unexamined applications; treat items that appear novel/unobvious as invention information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of unsearched patent documents
rubrics_metrics.description: All claimed subject matter that is potentially novel and unobvious in the opinion of the classifier who is an expert in the art must be classified as invention information along with any potentially novel and unobvious constituents or components (subcombinations) of the claimed subject matter. Any unclaimed subject matter in the disclosure that is potentially novel and unobvious in the opinion of the expert classifier must also be classified. For classifiers who are not experts in the relevant technical field, all the claims must be used for determining the subject matter to be classified. It is desirable to classify or index any additional information complementing the invention information if useful for search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When no search is available, rely on the classifier's expert judgment; if not an expert, conservatively classify all claims. Use discretion to add additional indexing/classification for helpful information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate classification of different inventive things within a document
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent documents should not be classified as a single entity, but all different inventive things, claimed or disclosed within the patent document, should be identified and separately classified. Such different inventive things are represented by different claims, alternative variants or different categories of subject matter (for example, a product and a method of its production).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and separately classify each inventive thing (including alternative embodiments and different categories). This ensures searchers can find distinct inventions contained in the same document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid duplicate classification symbols for same group (131bis)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two or more inventive things in a document separately are covered by the same group, the classification symbol of that group is allotted only once. If an inventive thing is appropriate for invention information classification in a certain group and another thing in the same patent document is appropriate for additional information classification in the same group, only the invention information classification is allotted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not repeat the same symbol multiple times for different inventive things; preference is to list invention-information classification over additional-information for the same group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unclaimed subject matter already classified in related application (exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unclaimed subject matter representing invention information does not need to be classified when fully identified in the classification of a related published application of the same patent office (for example, in the parent of a published divisional application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a related (e.g., parent) published application already fully identifies and classifies the unclaimed subject matter, do not duplicate classification in the related document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum classification if no invention information determined
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a classifier determines that no invention information is present within a patent document, at least one classification symbol must still be assigned to the patent document as an invention information symbol. In these circumstances, the classification should be based on that portion of the total disclosure that the classifier determines as most useful for search purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always assign at least one invention-information symbol even when invention information is not apparent; choose the portion most useful for searching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review of classification upon grant to minimize unnecessary symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: To minimise potentially unnecessary classification symbols, the classification of a previously published application may be reviewed when the application is granted, searched, evaluated or abandoned, in order to confirm or alter its classification. However, some offices classify an application only once and do not reconsider classification when a patent is granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where practice permits, re-evaluate classification at grant or later stages to remove unnecessary symbols; be aware of office-specific practices where reclassification is not performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting a subclass using IPC hierarchical approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the IPC is hierarchical, a systematic approach using its hierarchical structure can be used step by step for determining the appropriate subclass: identify the relevant section, then the subsection and class, and under the selected class, the subclass which most satisfactorily covers the subject. Remember titles give only broad indication of scope and consult references and notes after subclass titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the hierarchy as primary method; verify scope by consulting subclass notes and hierarchically superior places before final selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative methods to determine subclass (Catchword index, text search, related docs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative methods for determining the relevant subclass include: (a) using an alphabetical Catchword Index to the IPC; (b) text searching in the IPC or Catchword Index; (c) reviewing classification symbols of patent documents most related to the subject (e.g., statistical analysis of documents found during a text search).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These methods may be more efficient and can lead to a more specific place, but their results must be verified against the hierarchical scope and applicable classification rules for consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check subclass/group scope and applicable general/special rules
rubrics_metrics.description: After identification of a subclass, check whether its scope is wide enough to cover the technical subject. Before selecting a main group and subgroup, check which of the three general classification rules (common rule, first place priority rule, last place priority rule) is used in the selected subclass and whether any special rules apply. In some subclasses different general rules apply in different parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always verify notes indicating which general rule is used; if a subclass uses a priority rule, follow it when selecting groups/subgroups. Where only one main group covers the subject, classify there regardless of general rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common rule (default) for selecting groups
rubrics_metrics.description: The common rule is the default classification rule in the IPC and is applied where priority rules or special rules are not specified. Classification should be made in all appropriate places (i.e., multiple classification). After selecting a subclass, review all main groups and subgroups to identify which provide for the technical subject, proceeding down the hierarchy until no further subgroup applies. Subject matter relating to a combination of constituent parts is primarily classified in a group that provides for the combination as a whole; if no specific place for a combination is provided, classify according to each of its subcombinations and consider separate classification of novel subcombinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exhaustive hierarchical checking under the common rule; classify combination-as-a-whole first, and separately classify novel subcombinations where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: First place priority rule
rubrics_metrics.description: In areas where the first place priority rule applies, at each hierarchical level classification is made in the first appropriate place. The subject is classified by successively locating the first group covering any portion of the subject until a subgroup at the deepest appropriate indentation level is selected. If subject relates to a combination and no specific place for the combination exists, classify in the first group that provides for at least one subcombination; novel subcombinations must also be separately classified following the first place priority rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the standardized top-to-bottom sequence embedded in the scheme; the rule yields consistent selection of the earliest appropriate group at each level. Verify subclass notes indicating the rule applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Last place priority rule
rubrics_metrics.description: In areas where the last place priority rule applies, at each hierarchical level classification is made in the last appropriate place. The subject is classified by successively locating the last group covering any portion of the subject until a subgroup at the deepest appropriate indentation level is selected. If the subject relates to a combination and no specific place exists, classify in the last group that provides for at least one subcombination; novel subcombinations must also be separately classified following the last place priority rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the bottom-most matching group at each hierarchical level where the last-place rule is in force. Check notes for which areas use the last place rule (examples: A61K, C08G, C10M).

rubrics_metrics.name: Special classification rules override general rules
rubrics_metrics.description: In a limited number of places special classification rules are used which override the general classification rules. Wherever special rules are used, they are clearly specified in notes at the places concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow explicit notes for special rules in specific groups/subclasses (example: C08L Note 2(b) — classify macromolecular compositions according to the macromolecular constituent(s) present in the highest proportion). Special rules take precedence over common/priority rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation order and formatting of classification symbols and indexing codes
rubrics_metrics.description: The order of classification symbols and indexing codes on patent documents is: (a) classification symbols representing invention information (the symbol which most adequately represents the invention should be listed first); (b) classification symbols representing secondary classification; (c) classification symbols representing additional information; (d) indexing codes. Symbols and codes are presented in tabular form, one symbol/code per line, following the order down columns. Version indicators and font styles denote whether classification is in full IPC or main groups only and whether symbols represent invention information (bold) or additional information (regular).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place version indicator after 'Int.Cl.' when classified at least partly in main groups only; when classifying in full IPC, include version indicators after each symbol. Convention: full IPC symbols in italics; main groups only in regular font; invention-information symbols in bold; additional-information symbols in regular. Replace older version indicators earlier than (2006.01) with (2006.01) as noted.
